_what: The Haunted House, turning 09 off The Outskirts: an empty warehouse at the end of the road with a haunted house built inside it out of plywood flats, and the work lights left on behind the set, so the only light in the house is what comes through the seams. Built by tools/make-haunted-house.py into haunted-house.html between hh:<part> markers. Somebody in our community asked for it in the Sandbox's suggestion box on 2026-10-27; Ryan's brief, 2026-10-28.
_who: The house, its drawing, its rooms and every sentence not in a quotation are ours, written for this room by Claude to Ryan's brief. Every quotation names who said it and where, and was read on the day in `read`.
_things: A THING IS SOMETHING SPOOKY SOMEBODY MADE, hidden in one place in the house and laid out in the list with the lights up. The house opened with things from our own street and our own pages, and one public domain engraving, because nobody has brought anything yet and we do not fill the house from memory of what people like. A thing from somebody in our community goes in with `whose` as they want to be named, `given` (the day they said yes) and `said_yes` (who said it), and comes out the moment they ask, deleted rather than hidden: Show Your Work's bench rule. Something somebody else made goes in as a link with their name on it, never as a copy of their picture; a picture is only ever public domain (`rights`, a page that says so) or the maker's own, under data/polaroids.json if it is a photograph.
_places: EVERY THING HAS ONE PLACE AND EVERY PLACE ONE THING. `room` is a room of the house, `look` is the words on the button that looks there. A place is a button with a name in words, so the hunt is the same hunt with a mouse, a keyboard or a screen reader: the Den's door rule. A place with nothing in it is refused, because looking somewhere and finding nothing is a let-down this house does not hand out.
_sources: Where every quotation was read. `mirror` sources are pages of ours, checked word for word against the Knowledge System mirror when it is on the machine. `web` sources are somebody else's pages, read on the day in `read`; Smithsonian Magazine answers a script with 403, so its article was read in the Internet Archive's copy, and the room says so. `brief` is Ryan's brief for this room.

lede.p: Past the last streetlight, at the end of the road, there is a warehouse nobody was using. Inside it, somebody built a house: plywood flats screwed to timber, gaffer tape over the joins, every wall painted by people who had never painted a wall to look old before and did it anyway. **The work lights are on behind the set.** Inside the house you never see them. You see only where their light comes through: the seams where two flats do not quite meet, the gap under a door, the cracks between the boards over a window.

Things are hidden in the house: spooky things from our own street and our own pages, and, as people bring them, haunted things our community has made and things we love. **There are two ways through it.** With the lights up, everything is laid out in one list you can scroll. With the lights down, it is a hunt: go from room to room and look in places, and what is hidden there turns up where you looked. Nothing jumps out, nothing makes a sound, and the house counts nothing you find.

Its channel on the CB is for haunted things: share a picture or a link of something spooky you made or love, and say what it is. Sign on and tune the radio to **This room** while you are in here, or open [the house’s channel](chat.html#haunted-house) on the chat page.

veil.p: Halloween is All Hallows’ Eve, the night before All Saints’ Day on the first of November. It sits on top of something much older: Samhain, at the end of the harvest, when the light half of the year turned into the dark half.

The old word for a threshold, the strip of floor in a doorway between one room and the next, is the Latin **limen**, and it is where liminal comes from. The folklorist Arnold van Gennep used the idea in 1909 for the middle of a rite of passage: the part where you have left one state and not yet arrived in the next. A doorway, dusk, the turn of the year.

This house is built out of that idea. Every wall is a flat, and every seam is a threshold with the light on the other side of it. **The other side is right there.** It is the work lights, and the people who built the house, sitting on upturned crates behind the parlour wall.

history.p: Chris Heller’s short history of the haunted house, for Smithsonian Magazine, starts in London. In 1802 Marie Tussaud showed the wax heads of the French Revolution’s guillotined, made from the death masks she had cast of them, and called her permanent show the Chamber of Horrors. Around the turn of the century the Grand Guignol theatre in Paris staged dismemberment on its stage. In 1915 a fairground at Liphook, in England, opened one of the first ghost houses.

The Halloween haunted house is American, and it arrived in the Great Depression at about the same time as trick-or-treat, as a way to stop young people’s pranks from turning into vandalism. Lisa Morton, who wrote *Trick or Treat: A History of Halloween*, put it plainly:

**The first ones were basements.** Families decorated their cellars and children went from house to house, from one scene to the next. A 1937 party pamphlet has fur and strips of raw liver on the walls, wet sponges hung from the ceiling, a crawl through a long dark tunnel, and at the end a black cardboard cat outlined in luminous paint.

Disneyland’s Haunted Mansion opened in 1969, its ghosts made with Pepper’s ghost, an old stage illusion of reflected light, and Morton calls it the start of the haunted attraction industry. Within a few years the Jaycees, the United States Junior Chamber, were raising money with haunted houses across the country, built by volunteers.

Then the professional houses came, with film tie-ins and advertising. A fire at a haunted house in New Jersey killed eight teenagers who could not get out. The rules got stricter, and many of the volunteer houses could not keep up. Larry Kirchner, of the Haunted House Association, told Heller:
That fire is why **every room in this house has its way out written in it**, and why the way out is never called anything but the way out.

made.p: Ryan remembers them on the outskirts of town, in warehouses that were usually empty, built by the people who turned up to build them.

This one is a set and does not hide it. You can see the screws in the flats, the timber jacks propping up the sides, the tape on the seams and the light coming through them. **That is the frightening part and the good part at once**: a few people with no budget made you feel something in the dark, and you can see exactly how. It is the same thing [Show Your Work](show-your-work.html) says about showing the work while it is still being made.

weird.p: **Eldritch** is an old Scots word for unearthly: in Robert Burns’s *Tam o’ Shanter*, in 1791, the witches give an eldritch skreech. Where its first half comes from is not settled. One guess is elf, and another is an old English root meaning foreign, strange, other. [H. P. Lovecraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H._P._Lovecraft) brought the word back into fashion, and much of the horror he made with it was his fear of people unlike himself.

That is the oldest trick in horror, and the cheapest: make the frightening thing somebody who is different. Disabled bodies, minds that work differently, queer people and strangers have all been made into the monster, and the freak show charged admission for it. Our own write-up for an evening of chimeras heard it happen in a video about monsters:
**Weird is the word we kept.** [Our Weird page](https://stimpunks.org/glossary/weird/) is a long argument for weird pride, and it quotes Ferrous, aka Oolong:

So this house is eldritch, and nobody in it is the monster. On Halloween everybody wears the strange, and here the different are the ones who built the place. Our Halloween playlist, two years ago, said it in four words:

rest.p: Samhain closed the harvest and opened the dark half of the year, when the fields rest.

Remembering belongs here too. Ryan’s brief names remembrance of ancestors, and the people we have lost are part of why a thin veil is a lovely idea rather than a frightening one. Other peoples keep their own days for their dead, in their own ways; this house does not borrow them.

On this street rest is owed, not earned, which is [the Healing Checkpoint](healing-checkpoint.html)’s whole argument. The house stays up all year, so there is no hurry. Come back in the spring if the dark half is for sleeping.

not_here.name: Nothing jumps out.
not_here.line: No sound, nothing moves at any setting, and nothing appears unless you looked for it. A haunted house is allowed to frighten people; this one does it slowly and you can always see the light.

not_here.name: A way out of every room.
not_here.line: Every room in the hunt ends with the way out: back to the road, or the lights up. It is never called a chicken exit, and leaving early is a real way through the house.

not_here.name: Nobody is the monster.
not_here.line: No madness, no asylum, no disabled body and no difference is the scare in here, however old the trick is.

not_here.name: Nothing counted.
not_here.line: No score, no tally of what you found, and the house never says how many things are left to find.

not_here.name: Nothing kept.
not_here.line: The house remembers nothing about you. What you found is put back when you leave, and the next visit starts with everything hidden again.
